blocks.text: The problem: noise adds up

blocks.html: Real circuits are never perfect. Every block adds a tiny error, called noise, because of:

Approach What happens after many blocks
Analog (every exact voltage matters) Errors pile up. The picture becomes blurry and wrong.
Digital (only “low” or “high” matters) Each block cleans the signal back to a perfect 0 or 1. Errors don’t pile up.

• Low voltage → read it as 0

blocks.text: Big ideas

blocks.html:
• Every computer computes, remembers and communicates.
  • A problem reaches hardware through layers: problem → algorithm → program → system software → instruction set → microarchitecture → logic → circuits → electrons. This course: logic up to a simple CPU.
  • Chips are built in levels (transistor → gate → module → chip → board → device) using abstraction.
  • Moore’s Law: transistors per chip double about every 2 years (1965 paper said every year; revised in 1975).
  • Information is stored as voltage (e.g. 0 V black, 1 V white).
  • Noise piles up in analog chains. The digital abstraction reads only low/high, so each block restores a clean signal.
  • V ≤ V_L → 0, V ≥ V_H → 1, between = forbidden zone.
  • Binary = 2 values. n bits → 2ⁿ values. Binary place values: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…
  • Other bases: hex digit = 4 bits (A–F = 10–15); any base → decimal by place values; unknown bases: test the options in the equation.
  • Boole (1854): logic as maths. Shannon (1937): logic with switches (series = AND, parallel = OR).
